name: Necrotising sialometaplasia
specialty: Oral medicine / Oral and maxillofacial surgery

clinicalPearls: A benign, self-limiting inflammatory condition of minor salivary glands that clinically and histologically mimics malignancy
It most often presents as a sudden crater-like ulcer of the hard palate, sometimes bilateral
The lesion is important chiefly because it can be mistaken for squamous cell carcinoma or a salivary malignancy
Preceding local ischaemic insults such as trauma, injection, surgery or smoking are commonly identified
Histology shows lobular necrosis with squamous metaplasia of ducts while preserving the lobular architecture
Recognition avoids unnecessary radical surgery, as the lesion heals spontaneously over weeks
reference.pathophysiology: Necrotising sialometaplasia is thought to result from ischaemic injury to the minor salivary glands, most often in the palate, following vascular compromise from trauma, local anaesthetic injection, surgery, pressure or smoking. The ischaemia causes acinar necrosis, and reparative squamous metaplasia of the salivary ducts follows. This combination of necrosis and metaplasia can closely resemble malignancy both clinically and microscopically, but the preserved lobular architecture indicates a benign reactive process.
additionalDifferentials: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma or other salivary malignancy
Deep fungal or other infective ulcer
Ulceration from vasculitis or other systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Incisional biopsy with experienced histopathological assessment
History of preceding local trauma, injection or surgery
Clinical follow-up to confirm spontaneous healing
Exclusion of malignancy and infective causes on histology
redFlags: Failure to heal within the expected weeks
Histological features favouring malignancy on expert review
Associated systemic features suggesting another cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, healing spontaneously over several weeks without specific treatment.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the clinical or histological picture as carcinoma and performing radical surgery
Failing to obtain expert histopathology review
Overlooking a preceding ischaemic insult in the history
Not arranging follow-up to confirm healing
references: Oral and maxillofacial surgery reference texts (standard reference)
